title: The Last-Mile Station Billboard
brief: A coffee chain's new hot Americano launches next week, and the owner wants the MRT City Hall Station billboard. Three quotes, three prices. Does anyone even look at it?

lines.text: Morning, {role}! Our hot Americano drops next week. Boss wants City Hall Station.
Three vendors, three quotes, and I'm still waiting to hear back about open slots.
Let's figure out where people actually look in the morning, then decide how big to go.
My boss only wants to know one thing: does anyone actually look at billboards?
City Hall Bus Terminal empties out by nine. Walk the station and tell me how to spend it.
I'm at A25 waiting on your first page. The City Hall crowd's gone by nine, so move.

steps.prompt: The budget only covers one month. How do we spend it at City Hall Station?

options.text: Take the whole wall in the passage to City Hall Bus Terminal for one big, photo-worthy visual.
options.feedback: The day after it goes up, the wall is all over text-post apps and Manager Wu's boss is thrilled. Store visits barely budge, and finance asks how the wall pays off.
options.insight: The 2018 book notes that Taiwan's public transit ridership grew 86% in ten years, yet OOH's share of ad spend fell. The bottlenecks: measurement, automated trading, and dynamic delivery.

options.text: Go digital and use foot-traffic data to pick slots: hot coffee at dawn, takeout when it rains.
options.feedback: At 7:30 the screens show hot Americano; when afternoon rain hits, they flip to a takeout deal. Daily reports, but you babysit the schedule and eat breakfast at ten.
options.insight: The book names three keys for Taiwan's outdoor ads to evolve: measurement, automated trading, and dynamic delivery. Dentsu Japan found digital already makes up nearly 40% of OOH worldwide.

options.text: Buy one billboard: scan to add us on LINE for a coffee coupon, then steer them to a nearby store.
options.feedback: The board is small, but the scan line runs from the City Hall Station exit to the store. Three days on, Manager Wu texts: 1,000+ new friends. The next campaign's yours.
options.insight: Dentsu Japan research: OOH plus mobile ads gets 2.2 times the ad recall of mobile alone. Posterscope research also finds 83% of shoppers saw an OOH ad in the 30 minutes before shopping.

title: The Data Says Sales Dropped
brief: A third-party report says searches for the client's foot cream have plunged, and HQ wants to boost ad spend right now. But is the report seeing the whole picture?

lines.text: {role}, HQ at “Itch Be Gone” is on the phone, and they're in a hurry.
A third-party report says search and online buzz both dropped. It says boost ads now.
The report only sees searches dropping. It's been sunny. Maybe nobody has athlete's foot?
Big data shows what's on the surface, not always the truth. Give me an answer by noon.
The Corner Convenience Store on Songshou Rd. sells it. Ask the clerk who's buying lately.

steps.hint: Songshou Rd. Corner Convenience Store: who's buying Itch Be Gone?

lines.text: “Itch Be Gone”? Barely anyone bought it last month, then this week a whole shelf sold out.
Why's it suddenly selling so well this week?
Five days of rain! Everyone's shoes are soaked. One uncle says his stuffy rain boots itch.
And lots of the older folks just come in and grab it. They never look anything up online.
A woman in a suit asked the same thing earlier, too. Said she was from another agency.

steps.prompt: Before heading back to A25, what do you tell HQ?

options.text: Follow the report: boost search and social ads and win the buzz back first.
options.feedback: Ads go up, searches bounce back fast, and HQ breathes easier. Two weeks later the rain stops, the extra spend never brings matching sales, and finance starts asking.
options.insight: The book warns of the “caveman effect”: draw conclusions only from the data that survives, and it's easy to mistake the surface for the truth. Big data isn't all the data.

options.text: Add weather data, rerun the model, and prove searches move with the number of rainy days.
options.feedback: Ah-Kai lays three years of rainy days over the search curve, and the lines nearly match. HQ drops the extra spend and asks about prepping for next year's rainy season.
options.insight: In the book's nail-fungus drug case, a consultant's report said fewer people had symptoms. That year simply had nearly 30% fewer rainy days than the last. The report missed the local environment.

options.text: Hit ten stores for exit interviews and a short survey, so buyers who never go online count too.
options.feedback: You and a coworker split ten stores; your shoes end up as wet as their feet. Many buyers never search online. For the first time, HQ sees its customers clearly.
options.insight: The book argues big data has to be paired with sample surveys, retail interviews, and small data to see the people who leave no footprint online.

title: Cookie Countdown
brief: Third-party cookies die within two years, but your pandemic-hit client wants the whole year's budget on traffic. At the budget meeting before noon, who do you win over?

lines.text: With the pandemic, my boss says put it all into traffic. Sales you can see are what count.
But I hear cookies are going away? Will we still find the audiences we're buying now?
{role}, us again. We pitched one last week too: all traffic, beautiful reports.
They'll keep getting harder to find. How much of your own member data do you have?
30,000+ LINE friends, but the data's split across stores, online, and support. Unmatched.
Last year's orders are at the Lanshan Plaza data lab. {role}, want a look first?

steps.hint: Go to Lanshan Plaza Data Lab and see if the client's data is usable

lines.text: Checked the order files. One person has three IDs: in store, on the site, on LINE.
I spend three days a week cleaning data. Barely any time left for actual modeling.
Matching them isn't impossible, but it's a real project, not something a tool fixes.

steps.prompt: The budget meeting starts in ten minutes. What's your proposal?

options.text: Go along with the boss: all traffic ads, and prop up this quarter's sales first.
options.feedback: Sales hold up this quarter, and the boss thanks you by name in the meeting. But audiences get pricier every month, and you know this trick won't work next year.
options.insight: The book notes that in early 2020, Google announced Chrome, with nearly 70% share in Taiwan, would phase out third-party cookies. Buying traffic on third-party audiences is a road that keeps narrowing.

options.text: Put 30% into LINE tagging and member linking, so stores and e-commerce see the same person.
options.feedback: Stores start asking shoppers to link LINE, and in week one people complain it's too many steps. You switch to a free sample at checkout, and the link rate slowly climbs.
options.insight: A case from the book: isobar brought Salesforce and a new membership program to 10/10. First week: 8,880 LINE friends and a 74.61% member link rate.

options.text: Propose a CDP, make customer lifetime value the yearly goal, and count brand and performance apart.
options.feedback: The boss's face falls at “sales won't improve right away this year,” but the lifetime value math wins out. You spend the next three months in cross-department meetings.
options.insight: The book cites Adidas: after finding 65% of sales came from brand campaigns, it shifted its brand-to-performance budget from 23:77 to 60:40. Don't let short-term, visible results lead you around.

title: An Ad That Doesn't Sell the Product
brief: A realty client wants a pandemic brand film; its sales team wants every service perk in 30 seconds. The Chillshan Creative Park studio is only ours until 4 PM.

lines.text: Perfect timing, {role}. “Elephant Mountain View Realty” changed the script again.
They want seven service promises in 30 seconds, plus the hotline number at the end.
Which one will viewers actually remember?
None. I want newlyweds outside the registry office. The house is on screen for one second.
But the client asks: how do they explain an ad that doesn't sell the product to the boss?
Nail this and page four of tonight's pitch is done. Your call.

steps.prompt: The studio goes back at four. Which version do we shoot today?

options.text: Use the sales team's script: all seven service promises spelled out, hotline at the end.
options.feedback: The client signs off on the spot and you wrap early. The film lands as perfectly average; the top comment asks what hours the hotline is staffed.
options.insight: The book says that after the pandemic, consumers hold brands to “higher expectations,” and authenticity and trust are the new edge. A list of selling points is hard to remember.

options.text: Tell a consumer story: shoot the couple, keep the house in the background, brand only at the end.
options.feedback: When the director calls cut, even the lighting crew is wiping their eyes. A week in, viewers say they only knew it was a realty ad at the end, and shares keep climbing.
options.insight: A case from the book: Sinyi Realty's “Trust and Happiness” deliberately sold nothing. Positive post-test lift hit 70%, versus past KPIs of 20 to 30%. It also won Taiwan's first Cannes Grand Prix.

options.text: Shoot both, cut one of each, run a small test, and let the data pick the hero spot.
options.feedback: You and the editor work past midnight on two cuts. The story cut wins on likability, the selling-point cut on clicks. After the report, the client lets the story lead.
options.insight: The book warns against mistaking “the surface” in data for “the truth”: high clicks don't mean high trust. What matters is whether viewers feel differently about the brand.

title: Are Green Products Really Pricier?
brief: Your client's eco refills are out, but the Shin Kong Mitsuki counter says shoppers only see price. How do you get people to pay a bit more without cries of greenwashing?

lines.text: Look, {role}. In a whole week, the refills sold less than half what the bottles did.
I know we need ESG, but shoppers only ask how much more the green one costs.
Do shoppers think it's too pricey, or too much hassle?
Both, I guess. What the counter hears most: refills mean pouring it yourself. What a pain.
My boss wants a plan next week. And don't let anyone say we're greenwashing. Please.
Manager Hsu, our proposal comes tomorrow. {role}, see you at the pitch tonight.

steps.prompt: The plan is due next week. Which path do you lead with?

options.text: Let price do the talking: second refill half off, plus a limited-time online discount.
options.feedback: Refills sell out over the weekend and Manager Hsu is delighted. Once the promo ends, sales drop right back, and someone on social asks: does green only count on sale?
options.insight: The book cites a Kantar survey: 85% of Taiwanese think eco products cost more, and 76% don't act because of convenience and cost. Price is a barrier, but not the whole story.

options.text: Do the math for shoppers: plastic and money saved per refill, printed on the shelf and the pack.
options.feedback: Three days of number-crunching, and the new pack hits shelves by month's end. Shoppers read it closely. At last, says the counter, someone asks about more than discounts.
options.insight: In the same survey, 71% said brands don't give them enough information. The book cites secondhand fashion site ThredUp, which says buying one pair of used jeans saves 638 days of drinking water.

options.text: Get shoppers involved: return empties at the counter for points, and host a refill station monthly.
options.feedback: The first refill day's line runs from the counter to Xiangti Avenue, kids racing to help moms pour. But staffing it monthly stretches the counter and your weekends thin.
options.insight: The book cites IKEA, which encourages customers to resell and recycle instead of buying, so they live out the brand's sustainability stance together.

title: Spot the Sixth Finger
brief: A drink stand's posters for a new drink are all AI-generated and go live at 8 AM tomorrow. Today at Lanshan Plaza, you're the last checkpoint.

lines.text: {role}, AI made the “No-Overtime Milk Tea” posters. Forty, live 8 AM tomorrow.
Three in, I had a headache. The hand next to the milk tea: count the fingers.
…Six.
One has a sign for a shop that doesn't exist. One looks a lot like a certain illustrator.
Their boss says AI is fast, so don't stall. With good prompts, a rerun takes half an hour.
Word is the rival's nine pages tonight are all AI. We at least can't have six fingers.

steps.prompt: Sixteen hours to launch. What do you do with these posters?

options.text: Reject them all and have the designers redraw. Not one AI poster goes live.
options.feedback: The designers pull an all-nighter and the posters go live on time, clean and fully on-brand. The client's boss grumbles: so we bought AI tools just for the heartache?
options.insight: The book says people with no art background can sketch with prompts, but AI makes “six fingers” and fakes what it doesn't know. Taste and quality control still take people.

options.text: Three human checks: fingers and text, shop names, infringement. Only what passes goes live.
options.feedback: Eleven of the forty get cut; the rest are fixed and go live on time. Ah-Kai saves the checklist as a template and says next time you just reuse it.
options.insight: The book warns that fake content and infringement can badly hurt a brand. Tighten review and add AI disclosure clauses to contracts. Getty Images sued Stability AI for copying 12 million images.

options.text: Post the twenty clean ones, use social listening to catch errors, and swap if anyone complains.
options.feedback: The drink launches on time to great first-day sales. At 10 PM someone circles the sixth finger by the cup, the comments turn into memes, and you reply all night.
options.insight: The book warns that once content gets cheap, verification costs explode: telling real from fake used to take a second; in the AI era it may take a minute, even an hour.

title: Old Neighborhood Walking Map
brief: A clothing brand opens a flagship in the old streets by Linginger St. Night Market, with budget for one opening. Will the street come alive, or just for three days?

lines.text: {role}, “One Less Piece” opens on Linginger Street next week. Budget for one launch.
Another big store, huh? The last one had lines for three days. Day four, nobody.
Ah-Cheng's with the business association. He knows who's close with who on this street.
Walk to the Earth God shrine on Fude St. first. The old alley shops are this area's soul.
Tonight's pitch needs a local page. Take care of the client and the neighbors both.

steps.hint: Walk the alleys to Fude St. Earth God Shrine. Note the old shops

lines.text: Young one, you made the walk. What did you see?
An ice shop, a watch shop, a 40-year-old fabric store, and afternoon-only tofu pudding.
These shops used to serve hundreds a night. Now young folks hit one stall and leave.
A big store here: will it pull people away, or bring the whole street some life?

steps.prompt: Back at the flagship. How do you spend the opening budget?

options.text: Go all in on the in-store launch: limited collab items and influencer livestreams for week one.
options.feedback: Opening day, the line reaches the Keelung Rd. corner and week-one sales break records. By week two the crowd's gone. The ice shop owner says the line blocked his door.
options.insight: The book warns against chasing only short-term traffic and performance. A brand is the platform where all marketing investment accumulates, so do things that keep adding up.

options.text: Map the old alley shops, collab with the fabric store, and give a tofu pudding coupon with purchase.
options.feedback: You and Mei-ling go door to door; the watch shop owner lectures you 30 minutes. Once it's printed, someone walks it from the flagship to the Earth God shrine on Fude St.
options.insight: A case from the book: UNIQLO's East District program teamed up with nearby shops, hit 105% of its sales target, and drew 2.2 times the prior year's visitors. 91% said the store would bring them to the area more.

options.text: Run a LINE stamp rally: visit five old shops for a discount, and build member data along the way.
options.feedback: Over a thousand join in week one, and the member list grows. But many older folks can't scan, so every day someone at an old shop is teaching seniors to add friends.
options.insight: The book calls first-party and member data the core of the low-cookie era, and reminds you customer experience must be inclusive, looking after older customers and those with set shopping habits.

title: Is TV Really Too Expensive?
brief: A food client's boss says TV costs too much and wants next year's budget all digital. The meeting is upstairs at Big Dawn Dome Broadcast Center in twenty minutes.

lines.text: {role}! Your client's boss is upstairs. He just said zero TV next year. Not a cent.
I'm not selling here, but half their customers are moms and elders cooking at home!
What's the boss's reasoning?
He says digital reports show conversions, but with TV, nobody knows who's watching.
I just came down from upstairs. The boss is pretty set. Good luck, {role}.
20 minutes left. The Wuxing St. breakfast shop does late-night food. Ride over and look.

steps.hint: Wuxing St. Corner Breakfast Shop: what's everyone watching on TV?

lines.text: Everyone's glued to their phones now, but switch on the TV and they still look up.
That soy sauce ad just now? Three tables sang along together.
Auntie, when you buy soy sauce, is it the phone or the TV that sways you?
Who has time to scroll? I buy all the soy sauce at home. My grandson just eats!

steps.prompt: Before you head up, what proposal do you take into the room?

options.text: Go all digital like the boss wants, let conversion reports talk, and put the savings into promos.
options.feedback: The boss is pleased; the meeting's over in ten minutes. Six months on, new-product awareness stalls, and most conversions come from regulars who'd have bought anyway.
options.insight: The book warns that digital ads aimed only at target groups miss people like “the elders who do the family shopping,” and algorithms favor whoever is easiest to convert.

options.text: Keep broad-reach TV for the brand, use digital for younger groups, and show the boss the CPM math.
options.feedback: You write 48 and 80~250 on the whiteboard, and the boss stares at the numbers a long time. He says TV can stay, but results get reviewed every quarter.
options.insight: Dentsu Group estimates that for audiences 30 and up, TV CPM runs about 48, while YouTube is usually 80~250. The book says the broader TV's reach, the lower its unit cost.

options.text: Hold off. Run a brand study with a control group to see how many new customers TV really brings.
options.feedback: The boss gives you one quarter to test. Until results come in, the whole quarter's sales pressure sits in your weekly reports.
options.insight: The book warns a good Brand Lift doesn't prove real impact. It may just “light up the people who already liked you.” Tell apart the ones who'd have bought anyway.

title: Overtime Night in the Agentic Era
brief: A client's AI returns agent made a customer angrier and angrier; screenshots are already on social. How far can an agent decide alone, and when should a human take over?

lines.text: {role}, still at A25? Support at “Buy First Select” just called, voice shaking.
A customer's bag is defective, two days past the return window. And it's cross-border.
The agent cited general policy, then flipped to the defect clause. It contradicted itself.
Finally the customer typed: “So can I return it or not?” The screenshot's on social now.
The client wants to know by 9 AM: where the agent's authority ends, when a human steps in.
The pitch client's already seated, and page nine is still blank. Handle this first.

steps.prompt: Send your recommendation before you pitch. How do you set the agent's permissions?

options.text: Loosen it: under a set amount, the agent approves refunds itself. No waiting.
options.feedback: Refunds speed up and support volume halves that week. At month's end, finance finds a batch of refunds gaming a loophole. The client wonders who the agent works for.
options.insight: The book splits agent permissions into four levels: observe/understand, recommend, decide, act. It warns more autonomy isn't always better; open it up step by step based on risk.

options.text: Handoff rule: when two or more policies collide, the agent stops, sums up, and passes to a human.
options.feedback: You and Ah-Kai finish the rules just before you go on. Tricky cases now go straight to support staff, who see the three conflicts at a glance. No starting over.
options.insight: A case from the book: after an update, a returns agent pauses and hands off whenever two or more policies collide, and satisfaction on those cases stopped falling off a cliff. The book says an agent's limits are designed, not defects.

options.text: Scale the agent back to lookups and suggestions, rewrite its tone, and send all returns to humans.
options.feedback: No more contradictory replies; the screenshots sink from view. But support is booked through next month. The support lead wants to buy you a late snack, and hit you.
options.insight: The book cites an analysis of 200 B2B AI projects. Those with a human in the loop beat full automation on ROI by 104%, with 4.3 times fewer major errors.
